name: Oxybutynin for sweating
lead: Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medication approved in the US in 1975 for overactive bladder. It is also used off-label to reduce excessive sweating, increasingly since the 2010s, by people who want to stop visible sweat marks, damp hands and clothing changes.[1] Less sweating is described as helping people feel more confident in social and professional settings.[2]

Wikipedia notes that, as of 2024, this use remains off-label because dosing and the full side-effect profile are not established.[1] Reference sources list oral anticholinergics such as oxybutynin among treatments for focal and generalized hyperhidrosis, alongside topical aluminium chloride, botulinum toxin, iontophoresis, microwave devices and surgery.[2] Side effects of the anticholinergic class include dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation and vision changes.[2]
Published studies include a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in depressed patients on sertraline, and several registered studies in hyperhidrosis and menopausal hot flashes.[3][4][5][6]
infobox: Oral; transdermal patch and gel for bladder uses [1]

paras: Overactive bladder is oxybutynin's main use. Wikipedia calls it first-line therapy, partly because of well-studied side effects and long-term efficacy, and notes it is also prescribed after bladder surgery for spasms and catheter discomfort; use for bedwetting in children has declined.[1]

Hyperhidrosis is excessive sweating beyond what the body needs for temperature regulation. Focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8 percent of the US population, and more than 80 percent of patients report moderate to severe emotional effects.[2] Oral anticholinergics including glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin are listed for both focal and generalized sweating, and taking them before anxiety-provoking events is said to help.[2] In looks-focused communities, oxybutynin is discussed as a way to reduce armpit stains and visible sweat.
Oxybutynin blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors. It is metabolised in the liver into N-desethyloxybutynin, an active metabolite thought to contribute much of its side effects [1].

Oral absorption occurs within about an hour; Wikipedia's text gives an elimination half-life of 2 to 5 hours while its infobox lists 12.4 to 13.2 hours, so sources conflict. Protein binding is 91 to 93 percent, and after oral immediate-release use plasma levels of N-desethyloxybutynin can reach up to six times those of the parent drug.[1] The drug is a racemate, and the (R)-enantiomer (aroxybutynin) is the more potent anticholinergic.[1]

Oxybutynin comes as instant-release and extended-release oral capsules, a transdermal patch (Oxytrol) that bypasses first-pass liver metabolism, and a topical gel (Gelnique).[1] Hyperhidrosis use is generally of oral formulations.

High-strength aluminium chloride products are the usual first-line topical, taking 3 to 5 days to work with irritation as the most common side effect. Botulinum toxin type A injections block sweat gland nerve signals for about 3 to 9 months. Topical glycopyrronium tosylate was FDA-approved in 2018 for primary axillary hyperhidrosis. Tap water iontophoresis is used for palms and soles, and one trial reported about an 80 percent reduction in sweating. Endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy relieves hand sweating in about 85 to 95 percent of people but compensatory sweating elsewhere is common, affecting 20 to 80 percent.[2]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 140 depressed patients treated with sertraline examined oxybutynin for the sweating that is a common effect of SSRIs; the abstract reports that oxybutynin reduces sweating [3]. Registered studies include a long-term study of 1,100 participants (started 2007) [4] and a phase 2 comparison with placebo in women with plantar hyperhidrosis (32 participants) [5]. Results of these registrations are not summarised in the available record.

A registered study of women in menopause treated with a non-hormonal therapy for hot flashes and night sweats (999 participants, started 2023) is also listed.[6] Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article groups oxybutynin with other oral anticholinergics without giving trial effect sizes.[2]

Common effects include dry mouth, constipation, dizziness and sleep problems; serious risks include urinary retention, heat stroke because reduced sweating impairs cooling, and delirium [1]. A large study linked cumulative anticholinergic use to dementia risk in people over 65 [1]. Contraindications include untreated narrow-angle glaucoma and gastrointestinal obstruction [1]. The heat risk is higher for older adults and people with conditions such as multiple sclerosis, and contraindications also include paralytic ileus, severe colitis, myasthenia gravis and urinary obstruction.[1]

Oxybutynin is a generic drug; in 2023 it was the 114th most commonly prescribed US medication with more than 5 million prescriptions.[1] It is prescription-only in the US (an OTC patch status is also listed), Canada, the EU and UK, and is Schedule 4 in Australia.[1]

timeline.event: Oxybutynin approved for medical use in the US [1].
Off-label use for hyperhidrosis becomes more common. [1]
Topical glycopyrronium tosylate is FDA-approved for axillary hyperhidrosis. [2]

card.summary: A bladder drug used off-label as a sweat blocker, with a placebo-controlled trial behind it and a full anticholinergic side-effect profile.
card.note: Off-label for sweating; anticholinergic side effects include heat stroke risk.

quick.overview:
Oxybutynin is a prescription anticholinergic drug approved for overactive bladder and prescribed off-label for excessive sweating. A 2012 double-blind trial reported reduced sweating in sertraline-treated patients.

As of 2024 its use for sweating remains off-label.
quick.mechanism: It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing the signal that activates sweat glands.
quick.risks: Dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, urinary retention, heat stroke and delirium are listed; a large study linked cumulative anticholinergic use to dementia risk in people over 65.

chain: Oxybutynin blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors on sweat glands
Less sweat produced across the body
Drier skin, fewer sweat marks on clothing, drier hands
angle.text: Taken by mouth, oxybutynin reduces the nerve signal that triggers sweating, so people with heavy sweating look and feel drier, with fewer visible sweat stains and damp palms. The effect is systemic and lasts while the drug is taken.
